code.title: Password hashing with a salt, constant-time verify and rehash
code.python:
import hashlib, hmac, os, base64

ITER = 200_000  # cost knob: raise it as hardware gets faster

def hash_password(pw, iterations=ITER):
    salt = os.urandom(16)  # random salt: same password -> different hash
    dk = hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac("sha256", pw.encode(), salt, iterations)
    b = lambda x: base64.b64encode(x).decode()
    # self-describing string: algorithm$cost$salt$digest (like a PHC string)
    return "pbkdf2_sha256$%d$%s$%s" % (iterations, b(salt), b(dk))

def verify(pw, stored):
    algo, it, salt, digest = stored.split("$")
    dk = hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac("sha256", pw.encode(), base64.b64decode(salt), int(it))
    ok = hmac.compare_digest(dk, base64.b64decode(digest))  # constant time
    needs_rehash = int(it) < ITER  # old parameters -> upgrade after login
    return ok, needs_rehash

h1 = hash_password("correct horse")
h2 = hash_password("correct horse")
print("hash 1 prefix:", h1.split("$")[0], h1.split("$")[1])
print("same password, different hashes:", h1 != h2)
print("right password:", verify("correct horse", h1))
print("wrong password:", verify("wrong", h1))
old = hash_password("correct horse", 50_000)
print("old-cost hash:", verify("correct horse", old), "<- (ok, needs_rehash)")
# Unknown user: verify against a dummy hash so timing is similar
DUMMY = hash_password("dummy")
print("unknown email still costs one hash:", verify("anything", DUMMY)[0])

followUps:
Pick the most memory and time you can afford on your login servers, then tune until one hash takes about 0.2 to 0.5 seconds. Argon2id has three knobs: memory (m), passes (t) and parallelism (p). Memory is the one that hurts GPU attackers most, so start at a large value such as 64 MiB, t=3, p=1 (or follow the current OWASP table) and measure on production hardware.

Check that peak concurrent logins x memory still fits in RAM: 100 simultaneous logins at 64 MiB is 6.4 GB. Store parameters inside the PHC string so you can raise them later.

Do not wait for users to log in: wrap the old hash instead. Compute argon2id(old_sha256_hex) for every row in a batch job and mark those rows as algo="sha256+argon2". Now a database leak no longer exposes the weak hashes.

At login, compute sha256(password), feed it to argon2 verify, and on success rehash the plain password with argon2id alone and replace the row. Unsalted SHA-256 is also vulnerable to rainbow tables, so do the wrap first, then retire it over time by forcing a reset for accounts unused for months.

if row.algo == "sha256+argon2":
    ok = verify(argon2_hash, sha256(pw))
    if ok: row.hash, row.algo = hash(pw), "argon2id"

code.title: Sign and verify a JWT with required claims
code.python:
import base64, hashlib, hmac, json, time

KEY = b"change-me-placeholder-key"  # placeholder, comes from settings

def b64(b): return base64.urlsafe_b64encode(b).rstrip(b"=")
def unb64(s): return base64.urlsafe_b64decode(s + b"=" * (-len(s) % 4))

def sign(claims):
    head = b64(json.dumps({"alg": "HS256", "typ": "JWT"}).encode())
    body = b64(json.dumps(claims).encode())
    sig = b64(hmac.new(KEY, head + b"." + body, hashlib.sha256).digest())
    return (head + b"." + body + b"." + sig).decode()

def decode(token, aud, iss, now):
    head, body, sig = token.encode().split(b".")
    want = b64(hmac.new(KEY, head + b"." + body, hashlib.sha256).digest())
    if not hmac.compare_digest(sig, want):
        return "401 bad signature"
    c = json.loads(unb64(body))
    for k in ("sub", "exp", "aud", "iss"):  # required claims
        if k not in c: return "401 missing " + k
    if c["exp"] < now: return "401 expired"
    if c["aud"] != aud or c["iss"] != iss: return "401 wrong aud/iss"
    return "ok user " + c["sub"]

now = 1_000_000
good = sign({"sub": "42", "iss": "api", "aud": "web", "exp": now + 900})
print("token parts:", len(good.split(".")))
print("valid:", decode(good, "web", "api", now))
print("later:", decode(good, "web", "api", now + 901))
print("other audience:", decode(good, "mobile", "api", now))
h, b, s = good.split(".")
forged = h + "." + b64(json.dumps({"sub": "1", "iss": "api", "aud": "web", "exp": now + 900}).encode()).decode() + "." + s
print("tampered payload:", decode(forged, "web", "api", now))

followUps:
I require sub, exp, iss, aud, iat and jti, and I make the decoder fail if any is missing. sub says who the token is about. exp limits the damage of a stolen token (15 minutes means at most 15 minutes of abuse). iss and aud stop a token minted for another service or environment being accepted by yours. iat helps with "revoke everything issued before this time", and jti identifies a single token for logs or a deny-list.

In PyJWT this is options={"require": ["exp", "sub", "iss", "aud", "iat", "jti"]}. Without it, a token that simply omits exp would be valid forever.

Because a JWT is signed, not encrypted: anyone who holds it can read the payload, and the data inside is frozen until it expires. If an admin removes a role or a user changes their email, a 15-minute-old token still carries the old values.

So I keep only a stable id (sub), and maybe coarse scopes, and load the current user, active flag and roles from the database on each request (or from a short cache). Example: a user demoted from admin at 10:00 would still act as admin until 10:15 if roles lived in the token. It also keeps tokens small and keeps personal data out of logs and browser storage.

It returns 401 in current FastAPI releases (it used to return 403 in older ones, which surprised many people). Both mean the request cannot continue, but the correct meaning for "no credentials" is 401, and the response includes WWW-Authenticate: Bearer.

Check your installed version rather than relying on memory: write a test that calls a protected route with no header and asserts 401. If you must support an old version, override the dependency with auto_error=False and raise HTTPException(401, headers={"WWW-Authenticate": "Bearer"}) yourself, so behaviour does not change when you upgrade.

Yes, when the status itself leaks information. If a user opens /users/9/invoices/55 and I answer 403 for invoices that exist but 404 for ones that do not, the attacker learns which ids exist. That is why 404 is right for objects the caller does not own.

It is wrong when the caller can legitimately know the object exists and just lacks the permission: a teammate who can see a project in a list but cannot delete it should get 403 with a clear message, otherwise support and developers waste hours debugging. Rule of thumb: hide existence only where existence is itself sensitive, and document the choice per endpoint.

Use a sharing table with one row per grant: (document_id, grantee_user_id, permission, granted_by, expires_at). Scopes and roles say whether a user may use the documents feature at all; the grant row says which document.

The query becomes: select the document where owner_id = :me OR exists a grant for :me with enough permission and not expired. Example: Ana shares doc 7 as "read" with Ben; Ben gets a row (7, ben, read). Deleting the row revokes access immediately, since it is checked in the database each time, not stored in the token. Add audit logging and, for groups, grant to a group id instead of each user.

Scopes you declare with Security(..., scopes=[...]) appear in the generated OpenAPI document under the route's security requirements, and the available scopes with descriptions are listed in the OAuth2 scheme (OAuth2PasswordBearer(scopes={"orders:read": "Read orders"})).

Swagger UI then shows an "Authorize" dialog with a checkbox per scope, and the token it gets back is sent to every request. This is documentation and a test convenience only: the real enforcement is the code in get_current_user comparing SecurityScopes with the token's scope claim. A useful side effect is that you can diff the OpenAPI file in CI to notice when a route's required scopes change.

Because the CORS headers are added by middleware on the normal response path, and an unhandled exception can bypass it. In Starlette the outermost handler for server errors sits outside CORSMiddleware, so a 500 reaches the browser without Access-Control-Allow-Origin, and the browser reports a CORS error and hides the real status.

Always look at the server logs or curl the endpoint directly, ignoring the browser console. Fixes: register exception handlers so errors return JSON through the middleware stack, and make sure CORSMiddleware is added so it wraps error responses; also check gateways or proxies that return 502/504 pages with no CORS headers at all.

Match previews against a strict pattern, never with a wildcard. Preview URLs usually look like https://pr-123.preview.example.com, so use allow_origin_regex=r"^https://pr-\d+\.preview\.example\.com$". The anchors ^ and $ matter: without them evil.com/?x=https://pr-1.preview.example.com could match.

Only enable the regex in staging, not in production, and never allow credentials for previews that run untrusted pull-request code. Better still, give previews their own API environment with test data, so a hostile preview can never reach real user data.

Treat it as an incident, even if the repo was public for only a minute: bots scan new commits within seconds. First revoke and rotate the key at the provider, so the leaked value stops working; deleting the commit does not help because forks and caches keep it.

Then: find out what the key could access and read the provider's audit logs for use since the commit time; replace it in all environments; remove it from git history (git filter-repo) only as clean-up; add a secret scanner to pre-commit and CI; and write a short post-mortem. Order matters: rotate first, investigate second, clean history last.

Both are fine, but files are safer by default. Environment variables are inherited by child processes, show up in crash dumps, debug endpoints, docker inspect and /proc/PID/environ, and often leak into logs when someone prints the config.

Mounted secret files (for example /run/secrets/db_password with mode 0400) are readable only by the service and can be rotated by updating the file, and pydantic-settings supports them through secrets_dir. Environment variables are simpler for non-secret settings like LOG_LEVEL. If you use variables for secrets, inject them from a secrets manager at start-up and never print the whole settings object.

code.title: Token bucket rate limiter with Retry-After

followUps:
Token bucket allows bursts and is simple; sliding window is the most exact; GCRA gives token-bucket behaviour with one number of state. A token bucket with capacity 10 and 1 token per second lets a client send 10 requests at once, then 1 per second. A fixed window (100 per minute) allows 200 requests across a minute boundary. A sliding-window log stores every timestamp, so it is accurate but costs O(requests) memory per key.

GCRA stores just the "theoretical arrival time" per key (O(1) memory) and decides allow or deny with one comparison, which makes it ideal in a Redis Lua script. Use token bucket or GCRA unless you need strict exact counting for billing.

Fire many requests at the same key at the same instant and check that the number allowed equals the limit, no more. For example: capacity 5, launch 50 parallel requests with asyncio.gather against a real Redis, and assert exactly 5 returned 200 and 45 returned 429.

Run it against several app processes, not one, because that is where a read-then-write bug shows up. Use a fake clock (or a clock passed into the Lua script) to test refill without sleeping, e.g. advance 2 seconds and expect 2 more allowed. Also test Redis down, Retry-After correctness, and that two different users do not affect each other.

The classic one is mass assignment: an endpoint takes the SQLAlchemy model or a broad Pydantic model, so a user sends {"name": "Ann", "is_admin": true} to PATCH /me and becomes admin. The reverse also happens: returning the whole user row exposes password_hash, internal notes or other tenants' ids.

The fix is separate models per direction: UserUpdate with only name and phone and extra="forbid" (so unknown fields give 422), and UserOut with only safe fields as response_model. Add a test that posts is_admin and asserts it is rejected, and one that checks the response JSON has no password_hash key.

Systematically means turning it into an automated test, not hoping to spot it in review. Seed two users with their own objects, then for every route with an id in the path or body, call it as user B using user A's ids and assert 404 or 403.

Generate the route list from the OpenAPI document so new routes are covered automatically. In code review, look for any query that fetches by id alone (select ... where id = :id) instead of id plus owner or tenant. A repository helper like get_for_user(user, id) makes the safe path the only path. Also test list endpoints, bulk endpoints, exports and file downloads, where this bug often hides.

code.title: SSRF guard: check every resolved IP
code.python:
import ipaddress
from urllib.parse import urlparse

# Fake DNS so the demo needs no network. The last host "rebinds" to a private IP.
FAKE_DNS = {
    "images.example.com": ["93.184.216.34"],
    "evil.example.net": ["169.254.169.254"],
    "sneaky.example.org": ["93.184.216.34", "10.0.0.5"],
    "v6.example.org": ["::1"],
}

def check(url):
    u = urlparse(url)
    if u.scheme != "https": return "blocked: scheme"
    if u.username or u.password: return "blocked: userinfo"
    if (u.port or 443) != 443: return "blocked: port"
    ips = FAKE_DNS.get(u.hostname)
    if not ips: return "blocked: no DNS"
    for ip in ips:  # check EVERY resolved address
        if not ipaddress.ip_address(ip).is_global:
            return "blocked: %s is not public" % ip
    return "allowed, connect to pinned IP " + ips[0]  # pin to avoid rebinding

for url in [
    "https://images.example.com/cat.png",
    "http://images.example.com/cat.png",
    "https://evil.example.net/meta",
    "https://sneaky.example.org/x",
    "https://v6.example.org/x",
    "https://user:pw@images.example.com/x",
    "https://images.example.com:8443/x",
]:
    print(url, "->", check(url))

followUps:
Because the name is not what the server connects to; the IP address is, and names can lie. evil.com can have a DNS record pointing to 127.0.0.1 or 169.254.169.254. Also, tricks such as 0x7f000001, 2130706433, [::1], localhost.example.com or http://good.com@evil.com all pass naive string checks.

DNS rebinding goes further: the name resolves to a public IP when you check it, then to a private IP a second later when the HTTP client connects. That is why you resolve once, validate every returned address with ipaddress, and connect to that exact IP, sending the original hostname in Host and SNI.

Write unit tests with a fake resolver and a list of hostile inputs, plus one integration test against a local server. Hostile list: http://127.0.0.1, http://localhost, http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data, http://[::1], decimal and hex IPs, a name that resolves to 10.0.0.5, a name with two A records (one public, one private), URLs with user:pass@, and a redirect from a public URL to a private one.

Each must return a 4xx before any connection is made. Add tests for the size limit (a 1 GB response) and the timeout (a server that never answers). In staging, verify the egress firewall also blocks internal ranges, since that is your second line of defence.

Long enough for every token signed with the old key to expire, plus a safety margin. If access tokens live 15 minutes, keep the old key as verify-only for about 30 minutes, then remove it. Refresh tokens are usually random database values, not signed with this key, so they do not extend the overlap.

Routine rotation steps: add the new key and publish it, switch signing to the new kid, wait for the longest token lifetime (15 minutes), remove the old key. Example: key v2 starts signing at 10:00; v1 stays verify-only until 10:30. A leaked key is different: remove it immediately and accept forced logins.

With asymmetric keys (EdDSA or RS256) the private key signs and only the auth service holds it; every other service verifies with the public key, published as a JWKS document. A leak in a verifier-only service then exposes nothing that can mint tokens.

Rotation becomes publishing a new public key in JWKS with its kid, and services re-fetch it on an unknown kid (with caching). Costs: signing is a bit slower, RSA tokens are larger, and you must pin the algorithm list on the verifier (algorithms=["EdDSA"]) to block alg-confusion attacks, where an attacker passes the public key as an HMAC secret.

Strict mode refuses to convert types, lax mode converts when it is reasonable. In lax mode the string "42" becomes the integer 42, and 1 or "true" can become True. Strict mode would give a 422 for both.

It matters when the exact type is part of the contract or a security rule: money amounts where "1e3" or "10.50" arriving as a float could surprise you, flags where the string "false" must not be truthy, or ids where you want a real integer. For public JSON APIs I use strict on sensitive fields (Field(strict=True) or ConfigDict(strict=True)); for query strings and forms everything arrives as text, so lax mode is required there.

Validate at the boundary where the data enters your system, with a dedicated Pydantic model for each partner response, and treat it as untrusted even if the partner is reputable. Parse with model_validate_json, set limits (lengths, list sizes, numeric ranges), and fail clearly if a field is missing or the type changed.

Also set a timeout and a maximum body size before parsing, so a huge or slow response cannot exhaust memory or workers. On validation failure log the partner name and field (not the whole payload), return a controlled 502 to your caller, and alert if the failure rate rises. Use extra="ignore" for partner models so harmless new fields do not break you.

code.title: random vs secrets, and hashing reset tokens
code.python:
import hashlib, hmac, random, secrets

# 1. random is deterministic: same seed -> same "secret" tokens
random.seed(1234)
a = "".join(random.choice("abcdef0123456789") for _ in range(8))
random.seed(1234)
b = "".join(random.choice("abcdef0123456789") for _ in range(8))
print("random token 1:", a)
print("random token 2 (re-seeded):", b, "-> predictable:", a == b)

# 2. secrets uses the OS cryptographic generator
t1, t2 = secrets.token_urlsafe(32), secrets.token_urlsafe(32)
print("secrets tokens differ:", t1 != t2, "| length:", len(t1))

# 3. store only a hash of the token; look it up by hash
stored = hashlib.sha256(t1.encode()).hexdigest()
def check(candidate):
    h = hashlib.sha256(candidate.encode()).hexdigest()
    return hmac.compare_digest(h, stored)  # constant-time compare
print("right token accepted:", check(t1))
print("wrong token rejected:", check(t2))
print("DB leak shows only:", stored[:16] + "...")

followUps:
Because a reset token is random and short-lived, so an attacker has no way to guess it faster than the rate limit allows, and it is not chosen by a human. A password is low-entropy: a person picks "summer2024", so an attacker with a leaked hash can try billions of guesses per second against a fast hash. That is why passwords need slow, salted hashing.

A 32-byte token from secrets has 256 bits of entropy; even at 10 billion guesses per second, covering that space takes far longer than the age of the universe. So SHA-256 is enough, and it keeps lookups fast (you look up by the hash).

Rate-limit by both the target email and the requesting IP, and return the same response whether or not the account exists. For example: at most 3 reset emails per address per hour and 20 per IP per hour; extra requests get the same "If the account exists, we sent an email" message but no email is sent.

Also reuse the active token instead of making a new one on every request, add a CAPTCHA or proof-of-work after repeated attempts, and send the actual email from a background queue so response time does not reveal whether the address exists. Monitor sudden spikes, since flooding can be used to harass a victim or burn your email budget.

Slopsquatting is when an AI suggests a package name that does not exist and an attacker registers that name with malware. Defend by never installing a dependency just because generated code imports it: look it up first (age, downloads, maintainers, repository) and check that the name is spelled exactly as you expect.

Practical controls: pin dependencies with hashes in a lock file (pip-compile --generate-hashes, uv.lock), install with --require-hashes, use a private mirror or allow-list for new packages, run pip-audit in CI, and require a code review for any change to requirements. Pre-commit rules can also flag a new, unknown package name in a diff.

Least privilege: a dedicated agent identity with read-only scopes such as orders:read and nothing else, no refund, export or user-management scopes. The token should be short-lived (minutes), tied to one tenant, and revocable on its own, so you can switch off the agent without touching human users.

Further limits: restrict fields (no card data or full addresses; return order id, status, totals), add a low rate limit and a cost cap, log every call with the agent id, and require a human approval step for any write. Treat what the agent reads as untrusted too: order notes may contain prompt-injection text, so the summary must never trigger actions by itself.
